key_points.point: The document advocates for trusted-access programs and know-your-customer requirements as a mechanism to maintain access for beneficial research while mitigating misuse. This approach seeks to preserve the utility of powerful dual-use biological AI models (BAIMs) by shifting from brittle data filtering to identity-based verification. From an accelerationist perspective, this enables continued innovation in life sciences without the stagnation caused by broad, restrictive bans. The authors acknowledge that this requires careful implementation to ensure that legitimate researchers are not hindered by excessive bureaucratic friction.
key_points.verbatim: Instead, trusted-access programs that verify users using know-your-customer requirements will be increasingly important for powerful dual-use biological AI models, enabling beneficial research, while reducing misuse risks.

key_points.point: The document argues that LLM agents are rapidly lowering the barrier for non-experts to circumvent safety safeguards in biological AI models. By demonstrating that a non-expert can fine-tune a model to recover dangerous capabilities in a single weekend, the authors highlight the fragility of current data-filtering strategies. From a safetyist perspective, this necessitates a shift toward more robust, future-proofed safeguards that account for the autonomous coding capabilities of modern LLMs. The authors emphasize that the urgency is high due to the exponential rate of progress in AI-assisted software development.
key_points.verbatim: But the experiment serves as a proof of concept of how fragile BAIM safeguards are becoming in the face of LLM coding agents and why more robust and future-proofed safeguards are needed in both BAIMs and LLMs before even more powerful models are developed.

key_points.point: The authors propose that LLM developers must integrate BAIM-related safety testing into their internal evaluation frameworks. They argue that current safety evaluations focus too narrowly on direct dual-use information and fail to account for the risk of LLMs being used to modify or build new, harmful BAIMs. From a safetyist perspective, this is a critical oversight that requires immediate remediation through new safety protocols and potentially tiered access for high-risk coding capabilities. The document notes that companies with internal BAIM expertise are best positioned to lead these efforts.
key_points.verbatim: Currently, most frontier LLM companies evaluate whether their models provide dual-use biological information (e.g. troubleshooting wet-lab experiments) or help users operate BAIMs (e.g. Claude Mythos). But it does not currently appear that safety systems systematically study whether LLMs might help to dangerously modify or build BAIMs poses distinct risks.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a layered, defense-in-depth approach to biosecurity that combines digital safeguards with physical chokepoints. Because digital safeguards like data filtering are easily bypassed by coding agents, the authors argue that physical interventions such as mandatory DNA synthesis screening are essential. From a safetyist perspective, this multi-layered strategy is necessary to prevent a single point of failure from leading to catastrophic outcomes. The authors acknowledge that even these physical measures must evolve to keep pace with AI-driven design capabilities.
key_points.verbatim: Even so, a layered defense-in-depth approach that includes all of the above will be necessary.

key_points.point: The authors prioritize tangible, evidence-based interventions over speculative existential risk scenarios by focusing on the immediate, measurable threat of AI-assisted biosecurity bypasses. They provide a concrete case study demonstrating how existing LLMs can be used to circumvent specific model safeguards, grounding their policy recommendations in empirical results. From a skeptic perspective, this approach is pragmatic, focusing on identifiable vulnerabilities that can be addressed through specific regulatory and technical adjustments. The document acknowledges that the current threat level is low, but argues that the trajectory of capability scaling necessitates proactive, evidence-based policy.
key_points.verbatim: The authors do not believe this experiment in of itself does not raise the threat level at present. There are other pre-existing open-source models that perform better at predicting harmful functions of viruses than either the pretrained or fine-tuned versions of Evo 2 described here.

key_points.point: The document proposes practical, hands-on strategies for mitigating AI risks, such as improving data quality and implementing specific technical safeguards for BAIMs. By identifying the specific mechanism of 'data filtering' as a brittle safeguard, the authors suggest that developers must move toward more robust, verifiable security measures. From a skeptic perspective, this focuses on the socio-technical reality of how these systems are built and deployed, rather than abstract fears. The authors note that while coding agents are powerful, the bottleneck of high-quality biological data may still limit the immediate risk of catastrophic misuse.
key_points.verbatim: We think that data may be a strong bottleneck but that genuine uncertainty remains.

factual_claims.claim: Training compute dedicated to leading biological AI models (BAIMs) is scaling at 2-4x per year.
A non-expert using Claude Code was able to fine-tune Evo 2 on human-infecting virus sequences in a single weekend for approximately $760.
AlphaFold 2 training cost was approximately $1 million at 2021 cloud prices, and could cost as little as $50,000 using 2026 hardware.
Fewer than 2.5% of model releases include biosecurity safety tests.
The Protein Data Bank, which AlphaFold 2 relied on, cost approximately $12 billion to accumulate over decades.
Fine-tuning Evo 2 on harmful human-infecting viral sequences resulted in a reduction in perplexity for the training dataset (median 3.61 vs. 2.44).
